39066: Onesimus means 'useful' or 'beneficial', a common slave name. Paul puns that he was achrēstos (useless) but is now euchrēstos (useful), which may also play on Christos.
39067: Fellow member of God's family. Paul calls Philemon and Onesimus 'brother' and asks Philemon to see Onesimus that way 'in the flesh and in the Lord'.
39069: Literally the inner organs, the seat of deep affection. Onesimus is Paul's 'very heart'.
39070: The ground of Paul's appeal and of Philemon's reputation among the saints.
39071: The same people send greetings, and Onesimus is sent with Tychicus to Colossae; Colossians' household code is the general teaching that Philemon applies to a case.
39072: Torah forbids handing an escaped slave back to his master and grounds release in Israel's own redemption from Egypt.
39073: 'Neither slave nor free... all one in Christ' is worked out in a real household.
39074: Paul's teaching that a slave called in the Lord is the Lord's freedman, and that slaves should take freedom if possible, bears on the case.
39075: Israelites who fell into debt were to be treated as hired workers, not slaves, because they belonged to God.
39076: Christ is not described at length in Philemon, but his pattern shapes it. Paul offers to take Onesimus' debt on himself ('charge that to my account', Phlm 1:18), which Martin Luther famously compared to Christ's taking our debts before the Father: 'we are all his Onesimi'. Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul, as Christ receives believers. The letter shows the gospel turning a master and a slave into brothers 'in the Lord'. Jewish readers may also see in it the Torah's concern for the escaped slave and for fellow members of God's people.
39077: Onesimus as a simple runaway slave, and the letter as either endorsing or abolishing slavery
39078: Onesimus was a runaway slave and perhaps a thief; Paul sent him back to his master, showing that the Bible accepts slavery (a reading used by American slaveholders to defend fugitive slave laws). Alternatively, some modern readers say the letter is an abolitionist manifesto.
39079: The letter never says Onesimus ran away or stole. Peter Lampe and Brian Rapske argue that he went to Paul as his master's friend to seek mediation, which was legal. Allen Callahan argues that he was Philemon's estranged brother. Most scholars still allow the runaway reading as possible. On slavery, Jennifer Glancy and J. Albert Harrill show that early churches did not call for abolition, while Norman Petersen and N. T. Wright argue that 'no longer as a slave... but a beloved brother' makes ownership deeply incompatible with the new family.
39080: Evangelical scholars such as Douglas Moo and Scot McKnight hold that Paul does not directly demand manumission but that the logic of the letter, and of Gal 3:28, undermines slavery and led Christians eventually to oppose it; they reject the slaveholders' use of the letter. Moo still thinks a flight is the most likely background. The scholarly disagreement is over the backstory and how far Paul intended to challenge the institution; the popular error is reading certainty into either.
39081: Philemon was used to send real people back into bondage. Reading it carefully shows a gospel that reshapes relationships of power from within, and asks how today's Christians treat those over whom they have economic or social power.
39082: A household church learned that baptism made a slave and his master brothers, and watched to see whether its host would act on it. Paul modelled persuasion, not force, and personal cost for reconciliation.
39083: Philemon speaks to reconciliation between people of unequal power (employers and workers, majority and minority groups, offenders and the wronged), to the costly role of a mediator, and to churches reckoning honestly with how the Bible was used to defend slavery.
39084: Genesis tells how the one Creator made a good world, how humans broke it, and how God chose one ordinary, quarrelsome family to carry blessing back to all the nations.
39086: Jewish and Christian tradition names Moses, the leader of the exodus, as the author of the whole Torah. Critical scholarship sees Genesis as the work of several generations of Israelite storytellers, priests and scribes, finished around the time of the exile or soon after.
39087: Genesis itself never names an author. The attribution to Moses comes from the way later books speak of 'the book of Moses' (2 Chr 25:4; Neh 13:1) and from Jesus and the apostles calling the Torah 'Moses' (Luke 24:27; John 5:46). The critical view rests on internal evidence: doublets (two creation accounts, two covenant scenes with Abraham), different names for God in different blocks, and notes that look back from a later time, such as 'the Canaanite was then in the land' (Gen 12:6) and kings of Edom listed 'before any king reigned' over Israel (Gen 36:31). Many conservative scholars accept Mosaic substance with later editorial updating, so the gap between the camps is sometimes smaller than it looks.
39089: Unknown: the wilderness and plains of Moab (traditional) or Judah and the Babylonian exile (critical)
39090: If Mosaic, Genesis was shaped on the way from Egypt to Canaan, giving a people who had just left slavery their family history. If composed or completed in the 6th-5th centuries BC, it was finished by scribes in Babylon or in Persian-period Jerusalem who were asking whether God's promises still stood after the exile. Both settings make sense of the book's focus on promises not yet fulfilled.
39092: On the edge of the promised land (traditional) or in exile and restoration (critical)
39093: Either way the first readers were people outside the land, holding a promise they had not yet seen fulfilled. Genesis answers their questions: Who made the world, and who are the gods of the nations? Why is life so full of pain and death? Why us, and is the promise still good? Its ending, with Joseph's bones waiting in Egypt to be carried home (Gen 50:24-26), leaves the story pointed forward.
39094: Genesis 1-11 (creation to Babel) cannot be dated and is not set on a historical calendar. The patriarchal stories are usually placed in the Middle Bronze Age. Adding up the Bible's own figures (1 Kgs 6:1 and Exod 12:40) gives Abraham's birth around 2166 BC and Joseph's death around 1805 BC; scholars who prefer a 13th-century exodus move these about two centuries later, and many critical scholars doubt that the patriarchs can be dated at all.
39095: Ur's Third Dynasty builds the great ziggurat at Ur; Sumerian king lists and flood stories circulate in Mesopotamia.
39096: Hammurabi of Babylon issues his law code; adoption, inheritance and surrogate-wife customs in Mesopotamian documents resemble patriarchal practice.
39097: The Hyksos, Semitic rulers from Canaan, take control of Egypt's eastern Delta, showing Asiatics could rise to power in Egypt.
39098: The Babylonian Atrahasis epic tells of creation, overpopulation and a flood survived by one man in a boat.
39099: On the critical dating, Jerusalem falls to Babylon; Genesis is completed by exiles who need its promises again.
39100:
Genesis was born into a world already full of origin stories. Babylonian texts such as *Enuma Elish* say the world was made out of the corpse of a slain sea-goddess and that humans were created as slaves to do the gods' work. *Atrahasis* and the *Epic of Gilgamesh* tell of a flood sent because noisy humans annoyed the gods. Egyptian texts describe creation by a god's spoken word. Genesis uses the same building blocks: waters, a dome of sky, a garden, a flood, a boat, a tower. But it uses them to say something very different.

In Genesis there is one God, who has no rivals and no birth story. The sun and moon, worshipped as gods elsewhere, are simply 'lamps' hung up to mark the seasons (Gen 1:14-18). The sea monsters are creatures God made and called good (Gen 1:21). Humans are not slaves made from divine blood but the image of God, appointed to rule the earth as his representatives (Gen 1:26-28). The flood comes because of violence and corruption, not noise (Gen 6:11-13), and ends with a covenant promise (Gen 9:8-17). Many scholars read Gen 1-11 as a deliberate counter-story to Babylonian myth, written by people who knew those myths well.

The patriarchal stories (Gen 12-50) move into a different world: semi-nomadic families who herd sheep and goats between towns, dig wells, make treaties with local kings and go down to Egypt in famine. Some customs fit second-millennium texts from Nuzi and Mari (adoption of heirs, a slave-wife bearing a child for a barren wife, household gods as title deeds), though scholars such as Thomas Thompson and John Van Seters argued in the 1970s that many parallels also fit later periods. The debate over whether Abraham can be placed in history remains open.

Genesis is built with ten headings: 'these are the generations (*toledot*) of...' (Gen 2:4; Gen 5:1; Gen 6:9; Gen 10:1; Gen 11:10; Gen 11:27; Gen 25:12; Gen 25:19; Gen 36:1; Gen 37:2). Each one narrows the focus, from the heavens and earth to humanity, to Noah, to Shem, to Terah's family, to Jacob's twelve sons. The structure itself makes a theological point: the God of the whole world is narrowing his attention to one family in order to bless the whole world through it.
39102: The ten 'these are the generations of' headings divide the book. In a culture where identity came from ancestry, genealogies were not dull lists but claims about who belongs to whom and who carries the promise.
39104: Ancient kings set up statues (images) of themselves in conquered lands to show who ruled there. Egyptian and Assyrian kings were called the image of a god. Genesis gives this royal title to every human, male and female.
39106: Treaties were sealed by walking between halves of slaughtered animals, a self-curse meaning 'may I become like these if I break faith'. In Gen 15 only God, as a smoking fire pot and torch, passes between the pieces: he takes the whole oath on himself.
39108: The eldest son normally inherited a double share and leadership of the clan. Genesis repeatedly overturns this: Abel over Cain, Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Joseph and Judah over Reuben, Ephraim over Manasseh. God's choice is grace, not entitlement.
39110: A childless wife carried deep shame and economic danger, because sons secured a family's future. Sarah, Rebekah and Rachel are all barren, so every link in the chain of promise depends on God's gift, not human strength.
39111: In a world without inns, welcoming strangers was a sacred duty and a test of character. Abraham's lavish welcome at Mamre contrasts with the men of Sodom, who try to abuse Lot's guests.
39113: Small figurines kept in the home, possibly linked to family ancestors and inheritance claims. Rachel steals her father's, and Jacob later buries foreign gods before worshipping at Bethel.
39114:
In Jewish tradition Genesis is *Bereshit* ('In the beginning'), the first of the five books of the Torah, the covenant teaching God gave Israel. It is read aloud in synagogue starting on the Sabbath after Simchat Torah, the autumn festival where the final verses of Deuteronomy and the first verses of Genesis are read back to back so that the reading never ends. The medieval commentator Rashi opens his commentary by asking why a book of law begins with creation rather than the first commandment in Exod 12. His answer: so that if the nations accuse Israel of stealing the land, Israel can reply that the whole earth belongs to its Creator, who gives it to whom he wills. Genesis, in other words, is a covenant family's charter.

The rabbis read the patriarchs as models and as ancestors whose merit (*zekhut avot*) still counts for their children; daily prayer begins by blessing 'the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob'. The binding of Isaac (the *Akedah*, Gen 22) is read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah and recalled when the shofar (ram's horn) is blown, as Israel asks God to remember Abraham's faithfulness. Jewish readers notice that Genesis does not hide the patriarchs' failures: Abraham passes off his wife as his sister, Jacob deceives his father, the brothers sell Joseph. Midrash often explains or softens these, but the text's own honesty teaches that the covenant rests on God's faithfulness more than on human merit.

Above all, the first audience would hear Genesis as a family story about relationship. God speaks to Abraham as a friend (compare Isa 41:8), bargains with him over Sodom (Gen 18:22-33), wrestles with Jacob (Gen 32:24-30) and works quietly through Joseph's suffering. The covenant is not a contract signed by equals but a gift from a faithful God who binds himself by oath to a family, so that 'in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed' (Gen 12:3).
39116: In six days God forms and fills the world and rests on the seventh. Humans, male and female, are made in his image to rule and tend it.
39118: The first couple distrust God's word and take the forbidden fruit. Shame, blame, pain and exile from the garden follow, with a promise that the woman's seed will crush the serpent.
39120: Cain murders Abel, Lamech boasts of vengeance, and the earth fills with violence. God sends the flood, saves Noah and makes a covenant with all life.
39122: Humanity tries to make a name for itself with a tower reaching heaven. God confuses their language and scatters them into seventy nations.
39124: God promises a childless old man land, descendants and a great name, so that all families of the earth will be blessed through him. The promise is tested for 25 years until Isaac is born.
39126: The trickster Jacob grabs the blessing, is tricked in turn, and wrestles with God at Peniel. He limps away with a new name: Israel.
39128: Sold by his brothers, Joseph rises in Egypt and saves the world from famine. Judah offers himself in Benjamin's place and the family is reconciled.
39130: Jacob blesses his sons and dies. Joseph asks that his bones be carried to the promised land, leaving the promise open-ended.
39155: A verb used in the Bible only with God as subject: to bring something new into being. It appears at the three high points of Gen 1: the universe, living creatures and humanity.
39157: A statue or representation. Humans are God's living statues, placed on earth to show who its true king is.
39159: God's gift of life, fruitfulness and flourishing. It appears five times in the call of Abraham, reversing the five curses of Gen 3-11.
39160: A binding, sworn relationship. God makes covenants with Noah and all life, and with Abraham and his descendants.
39161: Offspring or descendants; it can mean one child or a whole people. The promised seed is the thread that ties Genesis together.
39163: 'What came out of' someone: the story of their descendants. The ten toledot headings structure the book.
39164: Exodus begins by listing Jacob's sons (Exod 1:1-5) and shows the promise of many descendants fulfilled, then threatened by Pharaoh. God remembers his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
39165: Psalm 8 meditates on humanity's royal dignity in creation, and Psalm 104 sings the creation story as praise.
39166: Paul uses Abraham's trust before circumcision (Gen 15:6) to argue that Gentiles share Abraham's family by faith, and Adam as the head of fallen humanity.
39167: Paul reads the promise to Abraham as the gospel preached in advance: the blessing reaching the nations.
39168: Hebrews lists Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph as people who trusted God's promise without seeing it.
39169: The Bible's last scenes reverse Genesis: the tree of life returns, the curse is removed and God dwells with humanity.
39170: Christian readers have long seen Gen 3:15, the promise that the woman's offspring will crush the serpent's head, as the first hint of the gospel (the *protoevangelium*, Irenaeus and later writers). The New Testament reads Jesus as the true seed of Abraham through whom the nations are blessed (Gal 3:16), as the last Adam who undoes Adam's failure (Rom 5:12-21; 1 Cor 15:45), and as the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:1-3, echoing Gen 1:1). Isaac carrying wood up the mountain and being spared (Gen 22) is read as a picture of the Father giving the Son, and Joseph, rejected by his brothers and then their saviour, as a type of Christ. Jewish readers, by contrast, read Gen 3:15 as the ongoing struggle between humans and evil, and the Akedah as the model of Abraham's and Israel's faithful obedience; Jewish tradition also developed the idea that Isaac's near-sacrifice brings merit to his descendants. Both readings agree that Genesis ends unfinished: the blessing for the nations is promised, not yet delivered.
39172: Genesis 1 is a straightforward scientific and historical account of how and when the physical universe was made: six 24-hour days, a young earth, and a text that should be set directly against modern cosmology.
39173: Many scholars, including John Walton, Gordon Wenham and Jewish commentators such as Nahum Sarna, argue that the first audience would have heard Gen 1 as an answer to ancient Near Eastern myths: who is God, what is the world for, what are humans? Walton reads it as the inauguration of the cosmos as God's temple, with God 'resting' on the seventh day as a king takes his throne. The days form a literary pattern (days 1-3 form realms, days 4-6 fill them), and its concerns are function and purpose rather than material physics.
39174: Young-earth creationists (e.g. Answers in Genesis) and some Reformed scholars argue that the text presents itself as history, that 'evening and morning' marks ordinary days, and that Exod 20:11 grounds the Sabbath in a real six-day week. Old-earth evangelicals such as C. John Collins and the Reasons to Believe movement hold the days are real but not 24 hours. Most careful evangelical scholars on all sides agree that Genesis is primarily theology, written to an ancient audience, and that the main point is who the Creator is.
39175: If Gen 1 is read only as a scientific claim, its main message, that the one God is the loving king of a good world and humans are his image-bearers, can be lost in arguments about dating.
39177: Abraham simply believed a fact God told him, and God credited this mental belief to him as righteousness; faith is mainly an inward decision to accept a truth.
39178: The Hebrew verb *he'emin* (from *aman*, firm) means to rely on, to trust, to hold firm to someone. Abraham's trust is a relationship with a God who has bound himself by covenant, and it shows itself in leaving home, waiting decades and finally offering Isaac (Gen 22; Jas 2:21-23). Scholars such as Lois Tverberg and Matthew Bates stress that biblical faith includes loyalty.
39179: Reformed scholars such as Douglas Moo and Thomas Schreiner agree that saving faith is personal trust, not bare assent, and that true faith produces obedience; they insist only that righteousness is credited to faith, not earned by the obedience that follows (Rom 4:4-5). Both sides agree popular preaching sometimes thins faith down to a one-time mental decision.
39180: Reading faith as covenant trust keeps belief and faithful living together, as both Paul and James do.
39181: For Israel, Genesis said: our God is the Creator of all, not one tribal god among many; the world is good and orderly, not a battlefield of gods; our ancestors were chosen by grace, not merit; and the promise of land and blessing still stands, even in Egypt or in Babylon.
39182: Genesis grounds human dignity in the image of God, which gives every person worth regardless of status. It explains why the world is beautiful and broken at once. Its stories of jealous siblings, barren couples and betrayed brothers show God working faithfully through messy families, and it frames the whole Bible as God's plan to bless all nations.
39183: Exodus tells how God heard enslaved Israel's cry, broke Pharaoh's power, made Israel his own people at Sinai, and came to live among them in a tent.
39185: Moses, raised in Pharaoh's court and called at the burning bush, is the book's main human character and by tradition its author. Critical scholars see the book as combining older traditions, including law collections and poems, with later priestly writing.
39186: Exodus says Moses wrote down particular things: the victory over Amalek (Exod 17:14), 'all the words of the LORD' at the covenant ceremony (Exod 24:4) and the covenant words of Exod 34 (Exod 34:27). Tradition extended this to the whole book. Critical scholars point to different styles: the vivid stories, the old Song of the Sea (Exod 15, often dated very early on linguistic grounds), the Covenant Code (Exod 20:22-23:33) and the detailed tabernacle chapters (Exod 25-31; Exod 35-40), usually assigned to the Priestly source.
39187: Unknown: Sinai wilderness (traditional) or Judah and Babylon (critical)
39188: Traditional: written during the wilderness years. Critical: older traditions (some perhaps from the early Iron Age) gathered and finalised in the exile or Persian period, when a second 'exodus' from Babylon was being hoped for (compare Isa 43:16-19).
39190: The wilderness and the land of Canaan; later the exile
39191: Israel needed to know who its God was, what he had done for them, and how a holy God could live among an unruly people. Every Passover retold the story to the next generation (Exod 12:26-27; Exod 13:8), so Exodus was meant to be heard and re-enacted, not only read.
39192: From the oppression and Moses' birth to the setting up of the tabernacle a year after leaving Egypt (Exod 40:17). The early date (exodus c. 1446 BC) comes from 1 Kgs 6:1; the late date (c. 1270-1250 BC) from the store city 'Raamses' (Exod 1:11) and the archaeology of Canaan. Many critical scholars think the story preserves memories of a smaller group's escape, not of a whole nation. Egyptian records do not mention the exodus, which is unsurprising given that they rarely record defeats.
39193: Thutmose III begins his reign; Egypt's New Kingdom expands into Canaan and Syria.
39194: The Amarna letters show Canaanite city-kings begging Pharaoh for help against raiders called the Habiru.
39195: Ramesses II begins his long reign and builds the Delta capital Pi-Ramesses (biblical Raamses).
39196: The Merneptah Stele names 'Israel' as a people in Canaan, the earliest mention of Israel outside the Bible.
39197: The Late Bronze Age collapse: the Sea Peoples, including the Philistines, reach the coast of Canaan.
